title: the dice game
hook: stake after stake, the same short line: I have won; and Vidura warns that the winner is in danger too

segments.voice: Yesterday in the dice game, the talk before the first throw: a warning, a dare, a vow, and a pearl set in gold lost. Did you catch yourself saying you couldn't back down? Day seven hundred sixty-eight.
screen: `CALLED TO PLAY, I DON'T TURN BACK.`

segments.voice: There's a line in this part of the poem that keeps coming back, like a drumbeat. Yudhishthira names a stake. Shakuni throws. And then Shakuni says, in effect: I have won. Then again. And again. The poem repeats it until the words themselves begin to sound like a warning. Today we sit inside that drumbeat, and we listen to the one man in the hall who stands up and tries to stop it.
screen: `A LINE LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` → `I HAVE WON.` → `ONE MAN TRIES TO STOP IT.`

segments.voice: After the pearl, Yudhishthira reaches for the next stake. Treasure. Gold. A fine chariot. Servants. Elephants. Horses. Soldiers. Each time he describes what he's putting down, carefully, almost proudly, as if the quality of the stake could change the fall of the dice. Each time, the throw goes to Shakuni, and the same short sentence follows: I have won. Notice what that refrain does. It takes the suspense away. We stop asking who will win the throw. We start asking something harder: why doesn't he stop? Somebody in the hall asks it out loud. Vidura, the blind king's wise half-brother, turns to Dhritarashtra. In the telling, he gives him a picture. A man climbs high after honey, and he's so taken with the honey that he doesn't see the fall in front of him. That, Vidura says, is your son with the dice. He begs the king to stop the game while there's still a family left to save. Duryodhana answers Vidura with scorn. He accuses him of always speaking for the other side, against the very family that shelters him. And Dhritarashtra says nothing that stops the game. Here's what's striking. Vidura's honey picture isn't about Yudhishthira, the one losing. It's about Duryodhana, the one winning. In the poem's eyes, the winner is in danger too. Each throw won for him is a step nearer the edge, and he can't see it, because his hands are full of honey.
screen: `STAKE AFTER STAKE.` · `THE DRUMBEAT: I HAVE WON.` · `VIDURA: THE MAN WHO CLIMBS FOR HONEY.` · `DURYODHANA SCORNS THE WARNING.` · then, large: `THE WINNER IS IN DANGER TOO.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let the hands rest. Bring to mind something that's been going your way lately: an argument, a streak, a race at work, a game on your phone. Now, gently, look past the honey. What's at the edge you might not be seeing? A person, a cost, an evening you haven't been home. You don't have to fix anything. Just look, the way Vidura asked the king to look. If you pray, you can bring that edge into your prayer. If not, simply breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
The dice game. Stake after stake, the same short line, I have won, and Vidura warning that the one who's winning is in danger too.
Your line: the dice game. Today, when something is going your way, pause once and look for the edge: who's paying for your streak? Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Vidura's warnings in the dice hall are a place where teachers and storytellers often pause, and his image of the honey-gatherer is retold as a picture of desire that can't see its own danger.

fork.setup: you're Vidura. the game is going badly, and the blind king is listening. what do you do?
options: keep quiet; it isn't your game.
speak to the king and beg him to stop it.
fork.reveal: he gives Dhritarashtra the picture of a man reaching for honey who doesn't see the fall, and begs him to stop. Duryodhana scorns him, and the game goes on.

original.note: Sanskrit akṣa: a die, the piece thrown in the game.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long list of things lost.
what it means: a refrain that turns suspense into dread, and a warning aimed at the winner.
what a scholar hears: Vidura speaks to Dhritarashtra, not to the players, so the poem puts the power to stop the game with the blind king.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Yudhishthira's successive stakes and Shakuni's refrain; Vidura's warning to Dhritarashtra, the honey-gatherer image; Duryodhana's rebuke of Vidura)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the list of stakes (treasure, gold, chariot, servants, elephants, horses, soldiers); numbers in the text were left out on purpose.
Confirm Shakuni's refrain in Ganguli ('Lo, I have won!' or similar) and that the poem repeats it after each stake.
Confirm Vidura's honey-gatherer image (a man collecting honey who does not see the fall) and that it is applied to Duryodhana.
Duryodhana's rebuke of Vidura is summarized as 'always speaking for the other side, against the family that shelters him'; confirm the wording is fair to the text.
Original: akṣa as 'a die' is standard; confirm pronunciation guide.
howItsDone 'a favorite place' is a general claim; soften if a Keeper prefers.
Editor: review and teach follow 767's corrected first stake (a pearl set in gold); hook no longer tells the reader they feel dread; howItsDone drops 'a favorite place'.

Audit: 'each throw he takes' corrected, since Shakuni, not Duryodhana, throws the dice. Keeper may wish to add that Ganguli says Shakuni won 'by unfair means' at each throw; the script leaves the cheating implicit.
